idiom_name: no enforceable equivalent: translation-unit linkage plus a narrow header, or a runtime-checked opaque handle
implementation_notes: C has no access control inside or across translation units - the only compiler-enforced boundary is linkage, and a token type cannot be made unforgeable, because any caller can write a zero-initialised struct value, a pointer to an unrelated object or NULL, and a signature that demands a token still accepts the forgery. What replaces the classic structure is therefore file organisation: keep the implementation in one translation unit behind static functions over an opaque struct and publish only the narrow entry point, which is the translation-unit-sized version of the same idea. If the token must survive an ABI, make it an opaque handle that the owning module validates on every call - a runtime check rather than the passkey's compile-time grant.
pitfalls: A struct or pointer token is forgeable - zero value, arbitrary pointer, NULL - so the compiler cannot reject a call and the 'grant' is documentation.
Passing the token by pointer lets the caller keep, copy and resell it; C has no construction scope to restrict in the first place.
alternative: There is no compile-time equivalent, so use C's own boundary: keep the implementation in one translation unit (static functions over an opaque struct) and expose only the narrow entry point from the header, or make the token a runtime-checked opaque handle that only the owning module can create and validate on each call. Real isolation has to be a real boundary - a separate process, a capability handle whose validity is checked, or a service that never hands out its internals.
